title: Mutable vs Immutable: Python's Core Idea

scenes.line1: Is your data safe from surprise changes?
scenes.say: Ever changed a list and got weird bugs? Let's see why knowing mutable versus immutable types is core in Python.

scenes.label: Mutable
scenes.sub: Lists and dicts can be changed after creation.
scenes.say: Mutable types, like lists and dictionaries, can be changed in place after you make them.

scenes.label: Immutable
scenes.sub: Tuples and strings can't be changed after creation.
scenes.say: Immutable types, like tuples and strings, can't be changed once they're created.

rows.b: y points to the same list

scenes.say: Assignment doesn't copy objects. It just points another name to the same thing. If you change a mutable object, every reference sees that change.
Lists and tuples look similar, but lists are mutable and use square brackets. Tuples are immutable and use parentheses.

scenes.question: Does list.copy() copy everything?
scenes.wrong: Yes, it copies all nested objects.
scenes.right: No, it only copies the outer list. Nested objects are still shared.
scenes.say: Here's a classic trap: copying a list with list dot copy only copies the outer list. Any nested objects inside are still shared.
